segments.text: This orange is three numbers. Two hundred thirty, one hundred twenty, fifty. Send them to two screens, and you get two different oranges.
Up close, a screen can't make orange at all. Each pixel has three windows: red, green and blue.
Behind them are a white backlight, a layer of liquid crystal, and a sheet of colored filters.
The crystal is a twist. Turned one way, light gets through. Turned the other, it's blocked. Each number sets the angle.
Red almost fully open, green partway, blue just a crack. Too small to tell apart, they blend into orange.
A four K screen has almost twenty-five million of these windows, all reset sixty times a second.
But the numbers never say which red. They only say how far to open each window.
This panel has deeper filters. Same numbers, and the orange turns redder.
That's the color difference between your screens. Neither one is broken. They obey the same numbers, through different filters.
Color management fixes it. The image is tagged with the red it was made for, and the screen rewrites the numbers for its own filters.
